analysis.one_liner: Bans union-security agreements so workers can't be required to pay union fees.
analysis.headline: Despite 130 Republican sponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in the House Education and the Workforce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal labor law to prohibit contracts requiring employees to pay union dues or fees as a condition of employment, ending "union security" agreements under both the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act, which covers rail and airline workers. Supporters frame this as protecting workers' freedom to decline union membership. Its practical effect would be to weaken unions' funding, since employees could receive union-negotiated wages and benefits without paying for them. The bill never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers gain, because unions with less guaranteed funding bargain from a weaker position. Individual workers who do not want to support a union gain directly, since they could keep the full amount of the fees they would otherwise owe. Unions' political opponents also gain from a weaker labor movement.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the provisions of the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act that let employers and unions sign contracts requiring employees to join a union or pay dues and fees as a condition of employment, including payroll deduction of union dues for railroad workers.
It is presented as protecting the free choice of individual employees to form, join, or assist a labor organization, or to refrain from those activities.
Workers who currently pay agency fees without joining the union would keep that money, roughly several hundred dollars a year in fee-charging workplaces.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls mainly on unions, which lose the fees of the workers they are legally required to represent, and on the workers whose pay and benefits depend on union bargaining power; federal law requires unions to represent all employees in a bargaining unit whether or not they pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unions and the workers they represent

drawbacks.text: Unions must bargain on behalf of every employee in a workplace regardless of whether that employee pays dues; if nonpayment becomes free riding, union treasuries shrink and their capacity to negotiate pay, benefits, and safety protections declines — this is the mechanism economists cite when they find right-to-work laws associated with lower union membership and wages.

The bill applies nationwide, overriding the choices of the more than half of states that have not adopted right-to-work rules and of unions and employers who agreed to union-security clauses at the bargaining table.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some workers would keep money they now owe in fees, and no employee would be forced to fund a union. But the same people benefit from union-negotiated wages whether they pay or not, so the bill's main measurable effect is to shrink union funding and, with it, unions' bargaining strength — a benefit to employers that most unions and many workers would experience as a cost. The one-sided partisan sponsorship and the lack of any hearing on the economic effects made it a contested bill that received no serious legislative consideration.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King introduced the National Right-to-Work Act on January 28, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On April 29, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, and the action history shows no further movement.
The bill attracted 129 Republican cosponsors in addition to the sponsor, but the committee never scheduled it for consideration, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organized labor and the workers whose pay depends on union contracts are better off, since the funding rules that sustain union bargaining survived; employers who backed the bill did not get the national right-to-work law they sought.

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Right-to-Work Act to repeal federal union-security provisions.

for.name: 129 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it an all-Republican sponsorship of 130 members.

sides.party_line_note: All 130 sponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill went nowhere in the Republican-led committee — opposition came from inaction rather than any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would strip unions of the fees from workers they are legally required to represent, cutting their funding and bargaining power. Union members who benefit from union-negotiated pay would share that loss; workers who resent paying fees would gain.

industries.industry: Employers, especially in rail and airlines
industries.note: With unions weaker and poorer, employers would face less organized pressure over wages and working conditions; the Railway Labor Act provision targets railroad carriers' payroll-deduction agreements directly.
